307 │ - #emph[Gravity tilted relative to the surface normal $( theta_g eq.not 0 )$: Hydrodynamic focusing in wells] Equation~(#text([])) implies in this case that a stationary solution only exist for anisotropic surface shapes with $ chi > 3 / 2 | tan theta_g | . $<eq:Gammacrit> Furthermore, assuming Eq.~(@eq:Gammacrit) holds, we see from Eqs.~(@eq:Pfull) that the stationary orientation vector is itself tilted relative to the fluid surface normal ($p_x^(\*) eq.not 0$). A linearization of Eqs.~(@eq:DynPi) around the stationary state Eqs.~(@eq:Pfull) for arbitrary~$theta_g$ shows that such a tilted state is still linearly stable. This has important consequences for swimmers that are bound below a potentially curved fluid surface: Whenever embryos tilt relative to the surface above them, part of the thrust that is generated by ciliary beating is converted into translational motion parallel to the surface. The direction of this translation is set by the direction of the embryo tilt, which in turn is set by the orientation of gravity relative to the surface normal. From the sign of given in Eq.~(@eq:Px) it follows that the body axis tilt relative to the surface is always oriented such that, for a convexly curved fluid surface in a well, bound embryos tend to translate towards the center of the well~(#ref(<fig:StokesletHydrod>)c, right). Complementing the Stokeslet-mediated attraction, this hydrodynamic focusing additionally contributes to the accumulation of embryos and thereby supports the formation of even larger clusters.
